turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Knee playing up, is it?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, it's the right knee, and I'm seventy-one so I probably should have come sooner, but I kept thinking it would settle. It really grabs when I come down the back stairs at home, the wooden ones with the wobbly rail, and I have to hang on like I'm on a ladder.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee only?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right is the one I came about. The left gives a little niggle if I've been round the shops all morning, but I wouldn't have booked for the left, it's nothing beside the right.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Karen, her daughter. I drove her so she didn't have to do the stairs at the station.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, um, that's the annoying part. I cannot date it. It was last winter, or, well, actually it might have been the winter before that, and I couldn't tell you the month.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've asked her. She goes round in circles. I can't put a date on it either.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Worse coming down stairs?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Much worse coming down than going up. Going up I'm just a bit stiff at the first step, but coming down I take them one at a time, sideways sometimes, and if I rush because the kettle's boiled it really bites on the inside of the knee.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night-time?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I wake, usually round two, and the right knee is aching deep in the joint. Most nights this past fortnight. I shove a pillow under it and that takes the edge off, then I can get back to sleep, though I'm not what you'd call fresh.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've checked in the morning light, and it doesn't swell and it isn't red. It just looks like my usual knee.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Locking, or giving way?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No locking, and it hasn't given way under me. I'm slow on it, but it holds.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She tripped on the hose last week. That was the hose, not the knee buckling.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Voltaren gel from the chemist, the diclofenac one. I rub a decent blob into the right knee morning and night, I don't measure it. And when the stairs have been rotten I also take the diclofenac tablets you can buy at the counter, not a script.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablet strength, and how often?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac, twenty-five milligrams. One tablet, maybe two or three times in a week, not every day. I try not to take the tablet the same evening I've already put the gel on, but some nights they overlap and I know that's probably not clever.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach trouble with them?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no stomach problems. I have them with toast or a bit of yoghurt and I've been fine on that front.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The scale at the clinic last month said ninety-six kilos, and I'm one metre sixty-two, so yes, I'm heavier than I was. Before I retired from the library I sat in the low eighties, and the kilos crept on with the desk and then with not walking.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ninety-six kilos. That load goes straight through the knee.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Speaking of not moving, the freeway this morning was a car park. We sat by that big servo for ages and the bloke in front was eating a pie at the wheel.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): And the radio was the cricket from Adelaide, and I was trying to tell Karen what a slip cordon is, and she kept changing the station to some gardening show.

[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I still don't see why everyone claps a maiden over. Anyway the weather's supposed to turn this arvo, big storms coming up from the south, so we want to be home before the dog starts hiding.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Little Ollie, my grandson, he's cricket mad. He bowls a tennis ball down their hallway and takes out the photo frames, and his mum rings me to complain as if I taught him the grip, which I suppose I did.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He rang last night, under-tens won by four runs, and now he wants a new bat. That's the whole saga from the car. Nothing to do with the knee, before you ask.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): A few minutes, that's all. I get up, it's tight, I walk to the kettle, and by the time the tea's poured it's loosened. Not an hour of hobbling, just those first steps.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hips or back?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Hips are fine and the back is fine. It's just the knee.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said the stomach was fine.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I did say that, and I meant no pain in the tummy or being sick, but I do get heartburn. A burning behind the breastbone, a couple of times a week, worse if I lie down straight after tea. It's been a few months. Since about March I can place that one better than the knee, though I don't know if it's the tablets or just me.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything for the heartburn?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon, the liquid from the chemist. One dose after tea when it comes on, not every night. It helps enough that I haven't needed anything stronger, and I haven't mentioned it till now, which is silly of me.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll look. Tender on the inner side?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, ow, that's exactly the spot, the inside of the right knee, not the kneecap so much.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender medial joint line, right knee. No effusion. Flexion is limited at the end. Ligaments feel steady.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): It catches a little when you bend it that far, a small clunk more than a pain. The night-time one is a deep ache, different from that catch.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like osteoarthritis. Wear and tear in the right knee. Working impression only. I wouldn't call it definite without an X-ray.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Could the gel be giving her the heartburn?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can't say. Oral diclofenac can cause heartburn. Ease off those tablets.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, I'll leave the tablets alone. I'd rather the heartburn went than keep taking them two or three times a week. Can I keep the gel, though, because that actually dulls the stair pain for a few hours?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gel's fine. Morning and night, right knee only.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the morning one after my shower so it soaks in before the trousers go on, and the night one in my pyjamas, and the smell is a bit menthol but I've got used to it. I won't put it on the left, since you said right only.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Next options are physio, or a steroid injection into the knee. Not deciding that today.

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I'd rather not leap to a needle if some proper exercises might sort the stairs, but I'm not ruling it out. My neighbour had a knee injection and she was walking the dog the next month, though that's her knee, not mine.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She hates needles. She'll still do whatever you actually recommend, she just talks herself in circles first.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll park both. Physio or an injection only if it's still limiting you. Come back in six weeks and say which way you want to go. If the heartburn picks up, stop the tablets sooner and ring the clinic.
